en: Petavatthu, Uragavagga 11. Nāgapetavatthu The Story of the Naga-Peta Long ago, monks, there was a certain man who was a fisherman. He went out onto the water with his net and caught many fish. Having caught them, he threw them onto the bank and began to prepare them for cooking. At that time, a nāga king named Erakapatta lived in the great ocean. He had a retinue of many thousands of nāgas. As the sun rose, the nāga king emerged from the great ocean and went to the shore. Seeing the fisherman preparing the fish, he thought: "This man has caught many fish; if he cooks them, they will suffer. It would be well if I were to protect these fish. Then the nāga king Erakapatta, assuming the form of a young brahmin, approached the fisherman and said: "O fisherman, do not cook these fish; release them back into the water. The fisherman replied: "I have already prepared these fish for cooking; I cannot release them. A second time and a third time, the nāga king Erakapatta, in the form of a young brahmin, requested the same thing, but the fisherman refused each time. Then the nāga king Erakapatta, becoming angry and displeased, spoke thus to the fisherman: "If you do not release these fish, I shall cause you to suffer. The fisherman, being terrified, released the fish back into the water. Because of that deed, monks, after the passing away of his life, that fisherman was reborn in the world of the petas as a nāga-peta. He was born with a body like a fish, and he suffered the consequences of his own actions. Thus it was said: "By whatever evil deed one performs, one surely experiences its fruit. Having done what is unwholesome, one does not escape suffering; One must experience the result of that very action oneself. Thus ends the Nāgapetavatthu, the eleventh story in the Uragavagga of the Petavatthu.
“In front he proceeds with a tusker elephant,
in the middle with a chariot drawn by mules;
and behind, a maiden is led away in a palanquin.”
Illuminating all ten directions in every way,
you, however, with mallets in hand,
weep with faces contorted and limbs mangled and pierced.
“Having become human beings, what evil did you do,
that you now drink each other’s blood?
“The one who went ahead on the elephant— ”
By means of the elephant Seta and the fourfold army,
our eldest son was born;
having given gifts, he now rejoices in happiness.
He who was our middle son, riding in the middle of a chariot drawn by four well-trained mules;
Free from stinginess and generous, she shines resplendent.
That woman of wisdom, with eyes like those of a deer, who is later carried away in a palanquin.
She was our youngest daughter;
she rejoices happily with her share of the inheritance.
And these gifts they gave in the past—
With hearts full of confidence in the ascetics and brahmins,
while we ourselves were miserly and revilers of the ascetics and brahmins.
"Having given these away, they enjoy themselves, while we wither away like a cut reed.
"What is your food? What is your bedding?"
"And how do you, who are of such evil nature,
live? Having squandered happiness amidst abundant and inexhaustible wealth, you have now fallen into suffering."
“Having slaughtered one another,
we drink pus and blood;
having drunk much, we are not satisfied.”
"We do not give," thus do mortals lament; those who do not give,
having passed away, abide in Yama's realm.
Those who, having known and acquired wealth,
neither enjoy it nor perform meritorious deeds,
will arrive at the next world overcome by hunger and thirst.
Later, burning for a long time, they meditate [in hell];
having performed evil deeds,
they experience suffering with bitter results.
For wealth and grain are fleeting,
and life here is fleeting;
having understood these things as fleeting, one should know them for what they are.
A wise person should make a lamp.
Those people who understand thus are skilled in the Dhamma.
“They do not neglect giving,
having heard the word of the Arahants.
The Story of the Nāga-Peta, the eleventh.
